raw_case_text:
On November 13, 2023, a 56-year-old male was admitted to the Nephrology Department of Shaoxing Scecond Hospital (Shaoxing, China) for a 1-day history of fever and abdominal pain, along with cloudy dialysate. Upon further investigation, he disclosed buying fresh mutton at a local private farm and consuming mutton hotpot at home 3 days before the onset of symptoms. The individual, who has undergone PD for a decade as a result of end-stage renal disease stemming from IgA nephropathy, encountered two instances of peritonitis, the most recent of which took place half a year ago. He consistently follows the conventional Continuous Ambulatory Peritoneal Dialysis (CAPD) protocol, performing four exchanges of 2,000 ml of 1.5% PD solution per day.
Upon admission, the physical examination revealed blood pressure of 155/83 mmHg, body temperature of 38.9 C, diffuse abdominal moderate tenderness without rebound pain or muscle tension. Laboratory examination was as follows: white blood cell (WBC) count of 19.3 x 109 cells/L), neutrophils 83.1%, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, platelet count of 173 x 109/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 167.5 mg/L, procalcitonin (PCT) 61 ng/ml, albumin 28 g/L. The PD fluid appeared turbid with a pale yellow hue, and had a total WBC count of 22,136/mm3, with 95.7% neutrophils. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen showed a localized dilation and multiple exudative changes of the abdominal aorta (Figure 1). Based on the patient's clinical data, empiric treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam (intravenous, 4.5 g/dose, twice a day) and vancomycin (intraperitoneal, 1 g/dose, first day; 0.5 g/dose, second and third days) was initiated for a presumptive diagnosis of PD-associated peritonitis and abdominal aortitis.
However, after a period of 5 days, there was no improvement in the patient's clinical status, and analysis of multiple peritoneal dialysate samples revealed a WBC count exceeding 10,000/mm3, indicating potential ineffectiveness of empirical anti-infective treatment. On the fifth day of hospitalization, the automated blood culture system detected bacterial growth in the aerobicblood culture bottle and prompting transfer to a Columbia blood plate. Following a 24-h incubation period, Brucella melitensis was identified through automated microbiologic analysis (Figure 2). Meanwhile, Brucella melitensis was also isolated from the dialysate culture. Additionally, serum brucella agglutination test was markedly positive (titer: 1:1,000). The final diagnosis of were established 7 days after the patient were admitted to the hospital. Finally, the patient was diagnosed with brucella-associated peritonitis and aortitis, and treatment was adjusted to rifampicin (600 mg/dose, once a day) and doxycycline (100 mg/dose, twice a day) for 6 weeks. We suggest using the standard doses of oral doxycycline and rifampicin for PD patients, as the dosages of these medications do not require modification based on glomerular filtration rate. Furthermore, the decision not to remove the PD catheter was made based on the patient's strong preference to continue with CAPD and the patient's geographical distance from the hemodialysis center. On the 4th day following the modification of the treatment regimen, the patient's temperature normalized, abdominal pain eased, and peritoneal dialysate cleared. By the 7th day post-treatment adjustment, the WBC count in the peritoneal dialysate was recorded as 0 and abdominal CT revealed normal abdominal aorta (Figure 1). Now the patient is currently under ongoing clinical observation. Figure 3 illustrates the timeline for diagnosis and treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male on peritoneal dialysis presented with a 1-day history of fever, abdominal pain, and cloudy dialysate.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute fever, abdominal pain, and cloudy peritoneal dialysate 1 day prior to admission. Three days before symptom onset, he had purchased fresh mutton at a local private farm and consumed mutton hotpot at home.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) for 10 years (four exchanges of 2,000 mL of 1.5% PD solution daily). History of two previous episodes of peritonitis, the most recent occurring 6 months prior. Epidemiological exposure: purchase of fresh mutton from a private farm and consumption of mutton hotpot 3 days before symptom onset.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure: 155/83 mmHg, body temperature: 38.9 °C. Abdomen: diffuse moderate tenderness without rebound pain or muscle tension.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell (WBC) count: 19.3 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 83.1%), hemoglobin: 8.9 g/dL, platelet count: 173 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP): 167.5 mg/L, procalcitonin (PCT): 61 ng/mL, albumin: 28 g/L. Peritoneal dialysate: turbid with a pale yellow hue, total WBC count: 22,136/mm^3 (95.7% neutrophils); repeated dialysate analyses over the first 5 days showed persistent WBC count exceeding 10,000/mm^3.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen on admission revealed localized dilation and multiple exudative changes of the abdominal aorta. Follow-up abdominal CT on day 7 post-treatment adjustment showed normalization of the abdominal aorta.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Automated aerobic blood culture detected bacterial growth on day 5 of hospitalization, yielding Brucella melitensis on Columbia blood plate after 24-hour incubation; Brucella melitensis was concurrently isolated from peritoneal dialysate culture. Serum Brucella agglutination test was markedly positive with a titer of 1:1,000, establishing the diagnosis of Brucella-associated peritonitis and aortitis. Management and Outcome: Empirical therapy with IV piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g twice daily) and intraperitoneal vancomycin (1 g loading, then 0.5 g daily for 2 days) failed to improve symptoms or dialysate pleocytosis. Following confirmation, treatment was switched to oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks, with retention of the peritoneal dialysis catheter. By day 4 of targeted therapy, fever resolved, abdominal pain eased, and dialysate cleared. By day 7 post-adjustment, dialysate WBC count was 0/mm^3 and follow-up abdominal CT demonstrated complete resolution of aortitis.
